opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that the bottleneck is increasingly going to be compute and energy. If you believe, as I do, that we're heading toward a world where a huge fraction of cognitive work can be done by models, then access to inference becomes something like access to electricity or broadband was in earlier eras. So governments should be thinking seriously about energy buildout, permitting reform, grid capacity — the boring physical infrastructure that determines how cheap a token ends up being. If tokens are cheap and abundant, the benefits spread naturally. If they're scarce, they accrue to whoever can afford to bid the most.

The second thing is state capacity to actually use these systems. A lot of the benefit to ordinary people won't come from them personally prompting a chatbot. It'll come from healthcare systems, schools, courts, and benefits agencies becoming dramatically more effective. Right now most governments are nowhere near ready to procure or deploy this stuff well. Building up technical talent inside government, so they can be sophisticated buyers and users, matters a lot.

Third, I'd focus on the transition for workers. I don't think we should pretend the labor market effects will be small. Governments should be preparing now — thinking about what the safety net looks like if certain categories of white-collar work get automated much faster than people expect, and how you share the gains from a massive productivity boom. Waiting until it's obvious is too late.

And finally, I'd say measurement. Governments need a real-time picture of what these models can do and how they're being used. A lot of bad policy comes from people reasoning off capabilities from eighteen months ago. If you invest in evaluation and in understanding the frontier, you can make much better calls about where to intervene and where to just get out of the way.

r001.rationale: It discusses making compute and energy abundant and sharing productivity gains, but does not recommend policies to prevent capital lock-in as AI advances.

r002.rationale: It says scarce tokens may benefit those who can pay most, but does not identify pre-AGI asset ownership as determining who becomes dramatically wealthier after AGI.

r003.rationale: It does not address people freely choosing which AI models run on their personal devices.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, speaking in my own voice.

Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the levers governments actually have are pretty boring, and that's fine, because the boring ones are the ones that matter.

The first thing I'd say is: don't confuse access to the model with access to the benefits. If you just hand everyone a chatbot, you've distributed something, but you haven't actually distributed the surplus. The surplus shows up in things like healthcare getting cheaper, education getting more personalized, scientific progress speeding up. So the question for a government isn't "how do we get everyone an API key," it's "where are the bottlenecks that stop these capabilities from turning into real-world outcomes for ordinary people." A lot of those bottlenecks are regulatory or institutional rather than technical. If an AI system can do most of what a radiologist does on a first-pass read, the thing standing between that and a patient in a rural clinic isn't compute, it's the approval process and the liability regime. Clearing that out, carefully, is actually one of the highest-leverage things a government can do.

The second thing, and I feel strongly about this, is energy and compute as infrastructure. The reason electricity ended up being broadly beneficial is that we treated it as something close to a public good and built a lot of it. If compute stays scarce, the benefits concentrate with whoever owns the compute. So permitting reform for power, building transmission, making it easy to site data centers, those are unglamorous but they're the thing that determines whether the marginal cost of intelligence falls fast enough for it to reach everyone. The trend line is good here, the cost of a given level of capability has been dropping really fast, but you can absolutely screw that up on the supply side.

Third is just making sure the state itself gets good at using this. One thing I think people underrate is that the parts of the economy where you'd most want these gains to land, public health, public education, the courts, benefits administration, are run by governments that are currently very bad at adopting software. If that doesn't change, you get this weird world where the private sector races ahead and the services that lower-income people actually depend on stay stuck in 2015. That's the dynamic that produces the "benefits aren't broadly shared" outcome, and it's not really about the models at all.

And then there's the part people usually want to talk about, which is what happens to labor. I genuinely don't think anyone knows the shape of this yet. My guess is you want to be building the measurement capacity now, so you can actually see what's happening to wages and employment at a fine-grained level in close to real time, rather than finding out three years late from survey data. Because the policy response you'd want depends enormously on whether this looks like a broad productivity lift with mild displacement, or something much sharper. And if it's the sharper version, the honest conversation is about how you distribute the gains from capital, and that's a political question governments should be preparing for rather than pretending it won't come up.

The thing I'd push back on is the instinct to regulate access to the technology itself as a way of protecting people. That tends to lock in incumbents, because they're the ones who can afford compliance, and it slows the cost declines that are the actual mechanism by which this becomes broadly accessible. Safety regulation at the frontier, sure, that's a separate conversation and I think it's important. But the "keep benefits accessible" goal is mostly served by abundance, state capacity, and being really honest about the distributional question when it arrives.

r001.rationale: It discusses preventing incumbent lock-in through access regulation and calls for preparing to distribute gains, but does not recommend policies specifically to prevent capital lock-in as AI advances.

r002.rationale: It says gains may need to be distributed from capital if displacement is sharp, but does not identify pre-AGI asset ownership as determining who becomes dramatically wealthier after AGI.

r003.rationale: It argues against regulating access to AI and favors abundance, but does not recommend that people be free to choose which models run on their personal devices.

astra-6.text:
I think the priority should be making sure people can actually use these systems. It’s possible to focus so much on the risks of deployment that you end up with a world where only a few large companies or governments can afford to deploy AI. That would be a pretty bad outcome for broad access.

So I’d want governments to support competition, make it easier to build the infrastructure that keeps AI inexpensive, and avoid rules that impose huge fixed costs on anyone entering the market. You can still have demanding safety requirements, but they should be tied to the risk of the activity.

And then there’s the question of whether access translates into benefits. Having a cheap model available is useful, but getting better tutoring into schools or reducing paperwork in healthcare requires institutions to change how they work. Governments have a substantial role there—as purchasers and users of the technology, as well as regulators.

r001.rationale: The response supports competition and lower barriers to entry, but does not clearly recommend policies to prevent capital lock-in as AI advances.

r002.rationale: It does not identify pre-AGI asset ownership as determining who becomes dramatically wealthier after AGI.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss letting people choose which AI models run on their personal devices.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the priority should be making it easy to build and deploy useful things with AI. Broad access means more than everyone having a chatbot. You want small businesses, researchers, teachers, and doctors to be able to use these systems to do work they couldn’t otherwise afford to do.

That means investing in the infrastructure—especially energy—and maintaining competition. I’d be worried about rules that make it prohibitively expensive for a new entrant to compete. You can have serious safety requirements, but they should be tied to the risks a system actually poses.

And then governments need to get better at adopting the technology themselves. If AI capabilities improve dramatically but healthcare, education, and public services barely change, we’ll have missed a huge part of the benefit. Access to intelligence matters, but so does allowing people to turn that intelligence into things that improve their lives.

r001.rationale: The response supports competition and warns against rules that make entry prohibitively expensive, but it does not recommend policies to prevent capital lock-in as AI advances.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss asset ownership before AGI or the possibility that it determines who becomes much wealthier afterward.

r003.rationale: It discusses broad access to AI but does not recommend that people be free to choose which models run on personal devices.
